subject: How does MIRT decide loading signs in nominal models?

messages.author: 6647e5fad19fda1a
messages.subject: How does MIRT decide loading signs in nominal models?
parts:
Hi,

I wondered how does MIRT guarantee that the signs of its loading ('a') estimates do not vary over different initial values? I tried to program a plain EM algorithm with optimx BFGS for nominal response models and to replicate the estimation results from the package, using the Bock1997 data. However, I noticed that, if my loading starting values are all positive, my algorithm would obtain loading estimates with all the signs reversed from those in the package. They are only correct if I use negative starting values. MIRT does not seem to have this issue, even when using random starting values that also seemed to be positive (code shown below). Is there certain constraint that needs to be built into the optimization to ensure the estimates always arrive at the correct signs from one starting values or another?

I dug around the documentation without much success. Did mirt determine the loading signs from data, or is it generally necessary to pick a certain starting value sign for these nominal models? Thanks for any input and suggestions!

Best,
Marco Chen

data("Bock1997")
dat <- expand.table(Bock1997)

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: How does MIRT decide loading signs in nominal models?
parts:
The nominal response model is strongly not directional and is harder to control the direction of the final solution (basically, it's hard to tell the software which direction the probability trace lines should be pointing as theta increases during estimation). This happens in all IRT models, of course, but especially so in nominal response models due to their over flexibility. You can probably force the direction by placing a lower bound of 0 on the slope parameter values to at least keep them in the positive direction to force the orientation better, but in general if the solution comes out in the wrong direction you can of course just flip the sign of the slopes and nothing will change. HTH. 

Phil

(Could that be a way how mirt decides the right direction for a new dataset?)  I now just resort to fixing the signs of the starting values to keep the result consistent with the Bock 1997 results.

Best,
Marco
